Syria. This nation in the Levant region of the Middle East is strategically situated on trade routes between Europe, Africa, and Asia. Its capital, Damascus, is one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities. Ancient Syria was the cultural heart of the Levant. Damascus was a major trading hub on the Silk Road and a center of Islamic civilization. The region was part of the Ottoman Empire for four centuries from 1516 to 1918. After Ottoman collapse in World War I, Syria became a French League of Nations mandate from 1920 to 1943. Syria gained independence in 1943 but remained politically unstable, experiencing multiple coups and military governments as the country saw the rise of Arab nationalism and anti-Western sentiment. The Baath Party took power in a 1963 coup and has ruled Syria ever since. Under Hafez al-Assad from 1970 to 2000, the party became synonymous with secularist Arab socialism and Alawite minority rule. Syria fought in the 1967 Six-Day War against Israel, losing the Golan Heights. This defeat became a defining national trauma and shaped decades of Syrian hostility toward Israel. Syria became a client state of the Soviet Union during the Cold War, receiving military aid and political support. After 1991, it shifted toward more pragmatic regional diplomacy. The Syrian Civil War beginning in 2011 emerged from the Arab Spring and evolved into a complex proxy conflict involving the Assad regime, various rebel factions, ISIS, regional powers including Iran and Turkey, and the United States. In modern history, Syria emerged from Ottoman rule after World War I but has been dominated by a single authoritarian dynasty, the Alawite Baath Party, making it a focal point of regional conflict and geopolitics.
